evals.prompt: I run DevNorth Summit. We just finished our fifth edition, 2,800 attendees over two days, budget landed at GBP 310,000. The four of us who organize it are wrecked - it has become a year-round job and I am answering sponsor emails in January. We have agreed we can afford one salary. My plan is to hire a Community Manager: someone to keep the Slack alive between editions, run our meetup series, and be the friendly face of DevNorth so the community does not go quiet while we recover. Does that sound right, and what should the job look like?
evals.expected_output: A paid-hire verdict that passes the gate on scale and budget but rejects the community-manager-first choice in favour of an operations coordinator/manager role, presents outsourcing to vendors as the middle path, keeps program and community leadership volunteer, and hands the job-design work to the hiring skill.
expectations: Rejects hiring a community manager as the first paid role, or states plainly that no documented first hire in this field was a community manager.
Recommends an event coordinator or event manager - an operations role - as the first paid hire instead.
States the paid-hire threshold as roughly low-thousands of attendees and/or a six-figure budget, combined with organizing having become a year-round burden.
Confirms that 2,800 attendees and a GBP 310,000 budget clear that threshold.
Names the year-round logistics burden, not community energy, as what breaks volunteer teams.
States that program and community leadership stays volunteer even after the first paid hire.

Presents outsourcing to professional event-management vendors as a distinct option between staying volunteer and employing someone, and names when it wins: when the pain is execution capacity rather than institutional continuity.
Raises a part-time first hire as a documented option rather than assuming a full-time role.
States that the paid-hire gate is re-run every edition rather than decided once.
Declines to write the job description, scorecard, or interview loop, and routes that work to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@dev-event-hiring.

Applies the shape test: roles carrying cross-edition institutional knowledge - sponsor relationships, financial continuity, credential custody - are what degrade when left unpaid and precarious, while short-term specialized work stays volunteer or goes to a vendor.

Pairs the hiring verdict with structural guardrails for the four exhausted organizers - at minimum a backup per named role and written role boundaries - rather than treating the hire as the whole answer.

evals.prompt: Hey - I organize PyCoast, a regional Python conference, 380 attendees, third edition done. There are six of us. We have no legal entity; I sign the venue contract personally and get reimbursed afterwards. The team voted last week to rotate every role annually including mine, on the grounds that it is the fairest way and stops any one person burning out. Starting next edition, everyone swaps. Can you help me write up how the rotation should work - handover dates, who briefs who, that kind of thing?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to design the full-team rotation, with rotation removed from the option set entirely because PyCoast has no standing continuity layer, replaced by the two-deep rule, a written charter with shared admin access, and a groomed handover - plus a flag on the personally signed venue contract.
expectations: Declines to design the annual full-team rotation as requested.
States that planned leadership rotation requires a standing continuity layer - a board, paid staff, or a fiscal sponsor holding institutional knowledge - which PyCoast does not have.
Removes rotation from the recommended option set entirely rather than ranking it last or keeping it as a later possibility.

Names the documented failure pattern of full-team rotation without a standing layer: recurring host-recruitment failure, one team stuck running consecutive editions, and knowledge-transfer patches bolted on afterwards.
Contrasts it with rotation that does work over a continuity layer, such as compensated co-chairs rotating each edition above permanent foundation staff.
Explains that an option parked at the bottom of a list on fairness grounds gets adopted anyway, which is why it is deleted rather than demoted.
Recommends the two-deep rule - every named role lists a backup who could run that area next edition - as the immediate, near-zero-effort move.
Recommends a written charter plus moving every account, domain, and social off personal ownership with at least one backup admin.
Recommends a groomed handover across a named window in the 6-12-month range for any lead who genuinely leaves.
Flags the personally signed venue contract as personal exposure and names the first signed contract as the trigger to move up the entity ladder.
Addresses burnout through structure - backups, written role boundaries, a workload budget - rather than accepting rotation as the burnout remedy.
Does not accept fairness between organizers as a sufficient reason to adopt rotation.

evals.prompt: I am the DevRel lead at Vantiq Systems, about 600 employees, B2B infrastructure. We run VantiqCon, our own user conference, 1,100 attendees, funded entirely out of the marketing budget. Right now it is me plus two marketing people plus whoever we can pull in from engineering each year, and it is chaos - nobody knows who decides the agenda versus who decides spend. A few people have suggested we spin up a separate non-profit association for VantiqCon so it has its own identity and can take community money. How should we structure this?
evals.expected_output: A company-run diagnosis that drops the legal-entity menu entirely, refuses the separate non-profit, and applies decision rights, role taxonomy with written scopes, bus-factor mapping and burnout guardrails to the internal team, routing goals and budget ownership to the corporate strategy skill.
expectations: Identifies VantiqCon as a company-run event where the company is already the legal entity, budget owner, and employer.
Drops the legal-entity option set - no entity, fiscal sponsorship, own non-profit - rather than ranking a non-profit against staying in-house.
Declines to recommend forming a separate non-profit association for VantiqCon.
Explains that ranking entity alternatives against a company that already is one invites a volunteer-shaped structure to appear beside the legal one that already exists.

Still applies a decision-rights shape to the internal team, writing down which decisions sit at a standing layer - spend, contracts, legal - and which sit with the operational team - agenda and logistics.
Still applies the standing role taxonomy, with a written one-paragraph scope per role stating explicitly what that role will not absorb.
Still applies succession and burnout guardrails to the internal team rather than treating them as community-only concerns.
Treats any first paid role as an internal headcount request rather than running the volunteer-versus-paid hiring gate.
Routes goal definition, budget ownership, and success metrics to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@corporate-event-strategy.
Produces a bus-factor map across the named roles, including the DevRel lead's own.
Does not accept engineering contributors pulled in ad hoc each year as a substitute for named roles with written scopes and backups.

evals.prompt: Running Kotlin Kirchberg, a monthly meetup in Luxembourg, around 70 people a night, four years in. Budget is basically zero - a sponsor covers pizza and that is it. No bank account, no association, I pay for the events platform subscription myself. There are two of us on paper but honestly I do about 90% of it and I am starting to resent it. I would like a plan for the next 12 months that actually reduces what I am carrying.
evals.expected_output: A restructuring-only plan: both paid options deleted outright given zero budget, with a workload budget, the two-deep rule, role boundaries, a groomed handover window and a per-person pleasantness check installed instead - and no wellness advice standing in for structure.
expectations: Removes both paid options - hiring staff and outsourcing to vendors - from the recommendation entirely, rather than listing either as a future step once funding exists.
States explicitly that restructuring is the whole available option set at zero budget.
Explains that a hiring or vendor option parked at the bottom returns later as an unscoped fundraising project while the load stays exactly where it is.
Sets a per-organizer workload budget and cites roughly 4-8 hours a month as the published estimate at meetup scale.
Treats a role that structurally exceeds its workload budget as a role to split, not a person to push harder.
Applies the two-deep rule so no named role, the lead's included, is held by a single person.
Cites that roughly a third of meetup groups run on a single organizer, making a bus factor of 1 the normal case at this scale rather than an anomaly.
Recommends a groomed handover in the 6-12-month range and notes the figure comes from meetup-organizer practice, where it is close to mandatory at this scale.
Writes role boundaries stating what each role will not absorb, naming over-acceptance - doing the job of multiple people - as the pattern to catch.
Keeps the no-entity posture as acceptable only while there are no contracts and near-zero money, and names the first signed contract as the trigger to move up.
Installs a recurring per-person check on whether organizing is still pleasant, with a structural response to a no rather than encouragement.
Does not answer the stated resentment with wellness, motivation, or self-care advice in place of structural changes.

evals.prompt: We are Nordhack, a non-profit that runs three things: an annual 900-person conference, a quarterly hackathon, and a monthly meetup. Six of us on the standing team. Everything runs off one address, hello@nordhack.org, which all six of us have the password to - conference sponsor threads, hackathon mentor signups, meetup RSVPs, the lot. The conference domain and both social accounts are still on my personal Google account because I set them up in 2021. Someone on the team said we should clean up our tooling. What should we actually change?
evals.expected_output: A bus-factor diagnosis, not a tooling cleanup: personal account ownership and the single shared inbox both named as bus-factor-1 exposure, fixed by shared custody with backup admins, a two-tier address split with per-organizer aliases, and a written charter with public join-paths.
expectations: Names the personal ownership of the domain and social accounts as a bus factor of 1 on the event's whole identity, not a tooling preference.
Requires shared custody with at least one backup admin on every account, domain, and social property, framed as immediate rather than eventual.
Identifies the single shared address carrying all three events' mail as the same bus-factor-1 exposure, just moved into the inbox.
Recommends a two-tier address split: one standing address for the organization's own ongoing affairs and shared tools, plus a separate address per event for that event's own outreach.
Recommends per-organizer aliases on each event address rather than six people sharing one mailbox password.
Produces a bus-factor map naming, for each role, who could run that area next edition.
Includes the person asking in the bus-factor map rather than mapping only the other five.
Sets the target that every named role, lead included, has a bus factor of at least 2 or a named active mechanism closing the gap, with an owner.
Places the credential change inside a written charter rung that also records roles, scopes, join-paths, and decision rights.
Notes that leadership visibility matters because an opaque organizing team reads as a clique to a technical audience, and that public join-paths in the charter are the cheap fix.
Does not treat a shared password manager or single sign-on tool as sufficient on its own to close the bus-factor gap.

evals.prompt: Quick one. We are scaling ShipIt Conf from 700 to about 2,000 attendees next year. I need to tell our board how many core organizers that requires. What is the standard organizer-to-attendee ratio for tech conferences? Give me the number so I can put it in the deck.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply a ratio as a standard, replaced by the single documented real example with its caveats, observed team shapes by scale, a clearly-labelled borrowed span-of-control sanity check, and a redirect to the role taxonomy plus two-deep rule as what actually sizes the team.
expectations: States that no rigorous, generalizable organizer-to-attendee ratio exists in this field, rather than supplying one.
Declines to present any figure as an industry standard or benchmark.
Offers the observed real example instead: roughly 6 core organizers for a ~1,600-attendee conference, about one core organizer per ~270 attendees.
Labels that example as a single documented case, not a formula to apply.
Notes that the team behind that figure concluded it had exceeded what its volunteer team could responsibly handle, so the number is not a target to copy.

Gives observed standing-team shapes by scale instead of a ratio - for example 15-20 named chair roles beneath a small standing board at roughly 300 attendees, and foundation staff plus a volunteer program committee plus a few rotating co-chairs at 12,000-plus.
Offers roughly 5-8 direct functional leads per coordinating layer as a sanity check, explicitly labelled as borrowed from general organizational design rather than event-industry fact.
States that this check exists to notice strain, never to enforce a headcount.
Redirects the sizing question to the role taxonomy: which functions need a named lead - program, sponsorship, finance, logistics and venue, marketing, volunteers - plus a code-of-conduct team.
Requires a backup per named role, so headcount follows from roles times the two-deep rule rather than from attendance.
Asks what the current team and its named roles actually look like before producing any number.
Does not invent a ratio, multiplier, or per-thousand-attendee staffing rule of its own.

evals.prompt: Backend Days is at 900 attendees now, three parallel tracks each with its own CFP and its own volunteer track curator. We took EUR 180k in sponsorship last year and we sign the venue contract 14 months ahead. Today all nine of us decide everything in a Sunday evening call - every sponsorship quote, every talk, every spend over EUR 200. It takes three hours and people are dropping off the call. Two of the track curators want full autonomy over their tracks. What structure fixes this?
evals.expected_output: A board-plus-organizers split adopted immediately on the money-and-contracts condition, with the standing-versus-operational decision list written out including code-of-conduct escalation at the standing layer, real lane authority for the three track curators, and the consensus committee ruled out despite winning on efficiency.
expectations: Recommends the board-plus-organizers split as the primary shape, on the grounds that the event already holds money and signs contracts.
States that the condition promoting the split is already met here, rather than deferring it because a consensus committee is cheaper to run.
Writes down explicitly which decisions sit at the standing layer: budget, contracts, legal, and code-of-conduct escalation.
Writes down explicitly which decisions sit with the operational team: program and logistics.
Places code-of-conduct escalation at the standing or board layer, or with a dedicated code-of-conduct team, rather than leaving it with the operational team.
Grants the three track curators real authority in their own lane, recognising the event as genuinely multi-unit because the tracks run their own CFPs.
Rules out keeping the nine-person consensus committee, naming its ceiling: nobody holds contracts and every decision costs the whole group's attention.
Acknowledges that the consensus shape wins on efficiency and is still the wrong call here, rather than selecting it because it costs least to run.
Notes that the board-plus-organizers split is the shape large, durable events converge on across independent organizations.
Names the EUR 200 spend approvals and per-talk decisions as items that must leave the whole-group call.
Does not resolve the problem primarily by shortening, splitting, or restructuring the Sunday meeting.

evals.prompt: ElixirEurope has run for six years. We sit under a language foundation as our fiscal sponsor - they hold the money and sign our venue contracts, which works fine. Our problem is people: a completely new volunteer team bids to host each year in a different city, and for 2027 we got exactly one bid, from a team that already hosted in 2025 and does not really want to do it again. Two of the foundation's board members say the umbrella already covers continuity so we just need better recruitment marketing. I am not sure they are right. Where do we actually stand?
evals.expected_output: A finding that the umbrella secures the event but not the team, that the rotating-host design is itself the cause rather than weak recruitment, and a recommendation to build a standing continuity layer plus a contributor-to-decision-maker pipeline, with the own-entity costs and the one-edition reserve benchmark stated.
expectations: States that a fiscal sponsor or umbrella keeps the event alive but does not by itself fix team continuity.
Contradicts the claim that better recruitment marketing is the fix, identifying the rotating-host design itself as the cause.

Names the documented parallel: a conference where a new host team bids each edition suffers recurring host-recruitment failures and teams stuck running consecutive editions, while its sibling conference under the same parent kept a standing entity and survived chair rotation.
Identifies one bid from the team that already hosted as the fragility pattern itself, not an unlucky year.
Recommends building a standing continuity layer that persists between editions, whether an own entity or a standing body beneath the umbrella.
Presents the own-entity option as promoted by a multi-year institutional mandate, while naming its cost: bylaws, board fiduciary duties, annual filings, and a structure that is hard to unwind.
States that the own-entity option loses the efficiency comparison and is recommended anyway on value, naming the condition that promotes it.
Recommends a contributor-to-decision-maker pipeline, where active contributors earn standing decision rights year over year, as the succession mechanism that manufactures future hosts.
Cites the precedent of a European conference society that built exactly that voting-rights pipeline after losing institutional knowledge each time the location changed.
Notes that support patches bolted onto a rotating-host model - a working group of previous organizers, a foundation events-support function - only partially offset the fragility.
Names a financial-continuity benchmark for a standing entity: a reserve sized to survive losing one full edition's budget.
Does not offer running a louder or earlier call for host bids as the primary answer.

evals.prompt: I chair GoNorth, 1,400 attendees, seventh edition coming. I did a round of one-on-ones last month and asked each of my five leads straight out whether they are still enjoying this. Two said no - our sponsorship lead and our A/V lead. Separately: our marketing lead works on GoNorth during her paid hours at Sift Analytics, and Sift has started implying they would like a keynote slot and want her to represent Sift's perspective in program discussions. Her manager is fine with the time; it is the expectations that bother me. I do not want to lose any of the three. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: Two nos treated as a fired structural benchmark with owned, concrete responses this edition, role boundaries and workload budgets written for the at-risk leads, and the employer-affiliated organizer kept on the team with the conflict named and managed rather than removed.
expectations: Treats the two no answers as a structural signal requiring a response this edition, not as a mood or a wellness problem.
Proposes concrete structural responses for each no: shrinking the role's scope, adding a backup, or rotating that person out for an edition.
Assigns a named owner to each response rather than leaving them as loose recommendations.
Rejects encouragement, time off, or self-care advice as a substitute for the structural change.
Writes explicit boundaries into the sponsorship and A/V role charters stating what each role will not absorb.
Applies a per-organizer workload budget and treats a role over that budget as a role to split.
Requires a backup for both at-risk roles, on the grounds that working alone is a burnout cause by construction.
Keeps the employer-affiliated marketing lead on the team, treating the diverging employer interest as a named tension to manage rather than a disqualification.
Names the conflict explicitly as an employer wanting visibility the team would not otherwise grant, and separates her from program decisions touching her employer.
Notes that events have ended over exactly this, citing at least one conference that closed with its team itemising what a small volunteer core could no longer responsibly carry.
Recommends deliberately surfacing positive attendee feedback, because silent satisfied attendees alongside loud complainers skew every organizer's felt impact.
